## 18. Closing out the points requested about T6b: the seventh connection identified (and it is not what the cert=None hypothesis suggested -- premise corrected), 28 JWTs/4 jwks/4 CA confirmed across the 4 profiles with no divergence, exact opin_flow.py diff with empirical proof of equivalence when V9_HARNESS is off

**1. The seventh mTLS connection, precisely identified.** I
instrumented `gateway/business.go`/`business_server.go` to log, per
connection, `remoteAddr` (the client's ephemeral port -- uniquely
identifies WHICH TCP connection served each request) together with
`clientCert` (the CommonName of the presented certificate, or
`"none"`) and `handshakeBytesIn/Out`; and I cross-checked this against
the HTTP access log, which now also carries the same `remoteAddr`.
Full round, Classical profile, complete list below (the same
structure repeats in the other 3 profiles, confirmed by sampling).

**Complete list of TLS connections for one run (insurance+person
combined), type and handshake bytes:**

| # | remoteAddr | SNI | Type | ClientCert | handshakeBytesIn/Out | What it served |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | :39996 | mtls | mTLS (cert required and presented) | classico_client | 1513/1640 | **nothing** -- see finding below |
| 2 | :40006 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /jwks(AS), /token, /jwks(RS), POST consents, GET consents x2, /request |
| 3 | :40020 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /root-ca.pem, /issuer-ca.pem |
| 4 | :56390 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /auth, /interaction x3, /auth/{id} |
| 5 | :56394 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /jwks(AS), /token, /jwks(RS), POST consents, GET consents, /request, /token(ac), 8x insurance-person |
| 6 | :56402 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /root-ca.pem, /issuer-ca.pem |
| 7 | :56414 | mtls | mTLS | classico_client | 1513/1640 | /auth, /interaction x4, /auth/{id} |
| -- | 7x :43xxx | matls-api.local | mTLS (internal, AS->RS) | op | 4307/2530 | `InsurerAdapter.getConsent()`, 3x insurance + 4x person |

**Finding: connection #1 (`:39996`) serves NO HTTP request at all --
it is the proxy's own readiness probe
(`_wait_for_tls_kem_proxy_ready()`, `opin_flow.py` line ~1179), which
makes a plain `GET /`, with no Host header recognizable by any
`ServeMux` pattern, receiving a 404 from Go's default handler -- which
in my code never passes through `loggingMiddleware` (only the
registered patterns, "auth.local/" etc., go through it), which is why
this connection opens (and shows up in the CONNECTION log) but never
appears in the ACCESS log.** This function is ALSO CALLED BY ME inside
the `V9_HARNESS` branch (same shared function, `opin_flow.py` line
1114) -- it is not a bug introduced by v9, it is the SAME mechanism the
real `tls_kem_proxy` has always had, exercised once per call to
`start_tls_kem_proxy()`, which both my test script and
`switch_crypto_profile.py` call once per combined run (the two flow
calls share the same proxy, started once before both).

**Excluding this probe, exactly 6 client-facing connections remain
(#2 through #7) -- v7/v8's historical number, matching exactly.** And
the 7 internal connections (`matls-api.local`) also match exactly
against what v8's `DECISIONS.md` Decision 77 had already found
independently ("7 internal AS-to-RS requests", same number, same
category). **Conclusion: there is no real count divergence. The "7" I
reported earlier was summing the readiness probe (which is not part
of the measured flow) with the 6 real connections -- an artifact of
MY OWN test script (which calls `start_tls_kem_proxy()` without the
care an official collection would take to exclude this connection from
the measurement window), not of the mechanism itself.** Recorded for
T7/T8: an official collection needs to start counting handshakes AFTER
`_wait_for_tls_kem_proxy_ready()` returns, not before -- this is
probably already how `switch_crypto_profile.py` operates in practice
(the probe happens during the profile's SETUP, outside the window of
any measured run), but this was not confirmed here.

**The `cert=None` hypothesis was wrong -- premise corrected, not
confirmed.** Connection #3 (`:40020`), which specifically serves
`/root-ca.pem`/`/issuer-ca.pem` (the call that uses `cert=None`),
**has `clientCert=classico_client`** -- a REAL client certificate was
presented and verified, exactly like all the others. Reason:
`requests.Session.request(..., cert=None)` does not turn off the
session's certificate -- the library itself (`merge_setting()`) treats
an explicitly `None` argument as "no override," falling back to
`session.cert` (which `run_insurance_flow`/`run_person_flow` already
set once, at the start, for all calls in that session).
`cert=None` in these specific calls never had the effect of turning
off the certificate -- it is only documentation/intent in the source
code, not real runtime behavior.

**Carve-out: NO endpoint waives the client certificate in v9 today --
a correction of the question's premise, not a description of
something already implemented.** Confirmed by the table above: the 7
client-facing connections (including those serving `/root-ca.pem`/
`/issuer-ca.pem`) have `ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert`
WITHOUT EXCEPTION, the same main config for the profile, across the 4
profiles, with no difference -- this is precisely the decision already
made and recorded in Decision 12 (closing v8's validity gap #3,
`VerifyClientCertIfGiven`, for ALL endpoints, not just some). If the
real v8 actually accepted a connection with no client certificate in
some case (possible, given it uses `VerifyClientCertIfGiven` globally),
this was never exercised by this specific flow (`opin_flow.py` always
sends a certificate, because of `session.cert` + the `merge_setting()`
behavior explained above) -- so there is, in this investigation's real
data, no historical v7/v8 call that was ever served without a client
certificate. **I did not create any new carve-out**, because the data
showed no need for one -- if Luciano wants v9 to deliberately
reproduce a "server with optional certificate" behavior for some
specific endpoint (reopening gap #3 just there), that is a new scope
decision, not a bug fix.

**Final classification for the metrics:** across the 4 profiles, 100%
of the 6 real client-facing connections (excluding the probe) ARE
mTLS with a client certificate -- zero server-only connections.
**v8's "6 mTLS connections" corresponds 1:1 to v9's "6 connections with
a client certificate"** -- there is no second category to split into,
because no server-only connection exists in the measured data.

**2. Remaining counts: 28 JWTs, 4 /jwks, 4 CA fetches -- extracted and
confirmed across the 4 profiles, ZERO divergence.** Extracted directly

## 19. Probe fix (confirmed with no loophole), internal carve-out documented, negative tests across the 4 profiles (16 scenarios, all correct), 5x5 interoperability matrix executed -- critical finding: the AND mechanism protects only in strict mode, confirmed at the pure TLS layer

**1. The readiness probe ALWAYS presents a client certificate -- there
is no loophole.** `_wait_for_tls_kem_proxy_ready()` does
`requests.get(url, timeout=1, verify=False)` -- a module-level call
with NO `cert=` at all, no Session, hence NO certificate on the LOCAL
leg (Python -> my proxy's local listener, which never requires one).
But my relay proxy (`relay.go`) builds `buildClientTLSConfig` ONCE, at
process startup, and uses that SAME config, with the profile's real
certificate, for EVERY accepted local connection -- including the
probe's. Confirmed directly in the log: the probe's connection
(`:39996` in that
Decision 18 round) shows up with `clientCert="classico_client"`, a
REAL certificate, verified by the gateway's `RequireAndVerifyClientCert`
like any other. There is no loophole because the two-hop architecture
(local leg with no certificate, real leg always with the process's
fixed certificate) is exactly what the real `tls_kem_proxy` has also
always done -- no change from v9 on this.

**Confirmed that the probe does NOT enter any measured counter.**
Bytes: the probe never reaches `loggingMiddleware` (404 from the
`ServeMux`'s default handler, which this middleware does not wrap), so
it never generates an ACCESS log line -- only the CONNECTION line
(which I added just for this diagnostic; the normal `measure`/T6 mode
does not log connections by default, it only uses the counter for
handshake_bytes, which is itself irrelevant here because this
connection was never part of any official measurement). Connections:
confirmed by the real `switch_crypto_profile.py`'s structure -- the
proxy is started ONCE per PROFILE SWITCH (not per run), and the probe
runs at that moment, BEFORE any of that profile's N measured runs
begin; the measured runs reuse the SAME already-probed proxy. **The
real v8 also excluded the probe from the "6" -- not through an
explicit filter, but structurally: the probe never happens INSIDE a
measured run's window, it happens only once, at the profile switch,
before the first one.** It was MY ad-hoc test script (which calls
`start_tls_kem_proxy()` on every call, simulating "every run is a
profile switch") that reintroduced the probe inside the window I was
measuring -- an artifact of MY OWN test method, not of the real
mechanism, already closed in Decision 18.

**2. Internal carve-out (`matls-api.local`), documented:**

| Aspect | Value |
|---|---|
| Authentication used | Pure classical TLS (CurvePreferences `[P521, P384, P256]`, negotiated `CurveP256` in the tests) -- never the main profile's hybrid/PQC group |
| Server certificate (my gateway) | ALWAYS the real `mock-service-os/certs/mtls.crt`/`.key` -- fixed, does not depend on v9's profile |
| Expected client certificate (auth) | `op.crt` (classic/hibrido-and) / `op_pqc.crt` (pqc) / `op_hybrid.crt` (hybrid) -- whatever `setup_ssm.sh` publishes for that real BACKEND `CRYPTO_PROFILE`, not v9's TLS profile |
| `ClientCAs` | always the real `ca.crt`; **plus** `root_ca_pqc.crt` when the profile is `pqc` (Decision 17, bug #2) -- the only variation between profiles |
| `VerifyPeerCertificate` | always `nil` (Decision 17, bug #3) -- never the main profile's AND/hybrid gate |
| Same across the 4 profiles? | The CODE that builds the carve-out is identical across all 4 (`attachInternalCallerCarveOut`, a single function, always called); the CA pool's CONTENT varies only under `pqc`, mirroring what the real backend publishes under that `CRYPTO_PROFILE` -- not a divergence among v9's 4 profiles, but the carve-out faithfully following what the real AS presents |
| Does it enter any measured counter? | Yes, as its OWN category ("internal connections", SNI `matls-api.local`) -- never added to client-facing connections. 7 per combined run, across the 4 profiles, matching exactly v8's Decision 77 ("7 internal AS-to-RS requests") |

**3. Negative tests, 4 profiles, 16 scenarios -- ALL correct (no
improper acceptance):**

Built in `thesis/results/v9/integration/negtest/` (new), run against
v9's REAL gateway/proxy binaries (not just the `dual_test.go` suite).
A methodological finding along the way, fixed before trusting any
result: a `Handshake()` that returns success on the CLIENT side is
not enough -- TLS 1.3 lets the client finish before the server
confirms its certificate, the SAME asymmetry `dual_test.go`'s
`dualHandshakePipe` had already documented and worked around in this
same session (T3). Without an extra read after `Handshake()`, the
first 3 profiles reported `UNEXPECTED_SUCCESS` for
`no-client-cert`/`untrusted-client-ca` -- WRONG, the server rejects
both, just the alert arrives later. Fixed (extra read,
2s deadline); final, clean result:

| Scenario | Classical | PQC | Hybrid-v8 | Hybrid-AND |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (i) no client certificate | REJECTED (`certificate required`) | REJECTED (`certificate required`) | REJECTED (`certificate required`) | REJECTED (`handshake failure`) |
| (ii) client certificate from an untrusted CA | REJECTED (`certificate required`\*) | REJECTED (`certificate required`\*) | REJECTED (`certificate required`\*) | REJECTED (`certificate required`\*) |
| (iii-a) server certificate from an untrusted CA | REJECTED (`signed by unknown authority`) | REJECTED (`signed by unknown authority`) | REJECTED (`signed by unknown authority`) | REJECTED (`signed by unknown authority`) |
| (iii-b) server certificate with the wrong SAN | REJECTED (`certificate is valid for [...], not not-a-real-san.invalid`) | REJECTED (idem) | REJECTED (idem) | REJECTED (idem) |
| (iv) Hybrid-AND, single RSA chain, STRICT mode | -- | -- | -- | REJECTED (`handshake failure`) |

\* The error reported for a certificate from an untrusted CA arrives
as the same `certificate_required` alert as scenario (i) in this
implementation -- Go's chain verification runs BEFORE the client's
`Handshake()` returns, so the observed alert is of the same class; the
rejection itself is real and confirmed (the client never
authenticates), only the alert text does not distinguish "no
certificate" from "certificate from the wrong CA" in these cases --
behavior of `crypto/tls` itself, not a bug in this implementation.

**4. Interoperability matrix, 5x5 (+1 critical row), now executed
locally -- long format, with the requested "effective AND protection"
column:**

| Client | Server | Success/Failure | Reason | Downgrade (DualAuthenticated) | Effective AND protection |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Classical | Classical | SUCCESS | correct group/cert (CurveP384) | n/a | n/a (does not involve AND) |
| Classical | PQC | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no (never authenticated) | n/a |
| Classical | Hybrid-v8 | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Classical | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | no Dual, server requires it (handshake failure) | no | **YES -- blocked a client with no PQ material** |
| Classical | Hybrid-AND non-strict | FAILURE | incompatible group, never even gets to test Dual (handshake failure) | no | not applicable (failed for a different reason first) |
| PQC | Classical | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| PQC | PQC | SUCCESS | correct group/cert (MLKEM1024) | n/a | n/a |
| PQC | Hybrid-v8 | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| PQC | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | no Dual, server requires it (handshake failure) | no | **YES** |
| PQC | Hybrid-AND non-strict | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | not applicable |
| Hybrid-v8 | Classical | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-v8 | PQC | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-v8 | Hybrid-v8 | SUCCESS | correct group/cert (SecP384r1MLKEM1024) | n/a | n/a (its own X.509 gate, not the TLS Dual) |
| Hybrid-v8 | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | no Dual, server requires it (handshake failure) | no | **YES** |
| Hybrid-v8 | Hybrid-AND non-strict | FAILURE | group matches, but Hybrid-v8's classical CA is not trusted by Hybrid-AND (`signed by unknown authority`) | no | **YES, but via classical chain verification, not specifically via Dual** (see note) |
| Hybrid-AND strict | Classical | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-AND strict | PQC | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-AND strict | Hybrid-v8 | FAILURE | group matches, but Hybrid-AND's ML-DSA CA does not exist in Hybrid-v8 (handshake failure) | no | n/a (not an AND test, it is chain incompatibility) |
| Hybrid-AND strict | Hybrid-AND strict | SUCCESS | both chains valid | **no -- `DualAuthenticated=true`, no downgrade** | **YES -- real dual proof of possession** |
| Hybrid-AND strict | Hybrid-AND non-strict | SUCCESS | both chains valid (client offered Dual, server accepted even without requiring it) | **no -- `DualAuthenticated=true`** | **YES -- non-strict did not WORSEN anything here, it just would not have STOPPED a weaker client** |
| Hybrid-AND non-strict | Classical | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-AND non-strict | PQC | FAILURE | incompatible group (handshake failure) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-AND non-strict | Hybrid-v8 | FAILURE | incompatible classical CA (`signed by unknown authority`) | no | n/a |
| Hybrid-AND non-strict | Hybrid-AND strict | SUCCESS | both chains valid | **no -- `DualAuthenticated=true`** | **YES** |
| Hybrid-AND non-strict | Hybrid-AND non-strict | SUCCESS | both chains valid | **no -- `DualAuthenticated=true`** | **YES, but by coincidence -- the client OFFERED Dual even without needing to** |
| **RSA-only (attacker), no Dual** | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | server requires Dual, client does not offer it (handshake failure) | no (never authenticated) | **YES -- blocked** |
| **RSA-only (attacker), no Dual** | **Hybrid-AND non-strict** | **SUCCESS (at the TLS layer)** | **server does not require Dual -- accepts the isolated classical chain** | **YES -- authenticated with `DualAuthenticated=false`, WITHOUT ever proving ML-DSA-65 possession** | **NO -- vulnerable, see critical finding below** |

**Critical finding, an extra row (not part of the original 5x5 matrix,
added because it is exactly what "effective AND protection" needs to
answer): an attacker with ONLY the RSA key (no PQ material at all,
`Dual=nil` on the client) was ACCEPTED, at the pure TLS layer, by the
NON-STRICT Hybrid-AND server.** Confirmed directly, with no
interpretation: the client's own `Handshake()` returned success --
`curve=SecP384r1MLKEM1024 dualAuthenticated=false` -- a complete,
valid TLS authentication, WITHOUT ever proving possession of the
ML-DSA-65 key. **This is, literally, the same vulnerability the real
v8 Hybrid has, and that this entire project exists to close** -- only
now reproduced and confirmed live inside the Dual mechanism itself, in
the mode that leaves it turned off. The connection just was NOT served
because MY test gateway (`measure` mode) has a second check, at the
APPLICATION layer (not the TLS protocol), that closes any `hibrido-and`
connection with `DualAuthenticated=false` regardless of the configured
`Require` -- an extra defense I wrote for the test harness, NOT a
property of the Dual mechanism itself. A real deployment that
configured `Dual.Require=false` without this additional check would
be genuinely vulnerable. **This definitively confirms, now measured
(not just argued), why strict mode is mandatory -- it is not a design
preference, it is the only configuration in which the dual
proof-of-possession guarantee truly exists in the protocol.**

**(e) Pilot tolerance for reproducing per-message sizes --
calculated, not assumed.** I regenerated the certificates with SANs
of the real size an AWS instance would have (EC2 public/private DNS,
`sa-east-1`, e.g., `ec2-18-230-105-42.sa-east-1.compute.amazonaws.com`/
`ip-10-0-1-134.sa-east-1.compute.internal`, plus 5 internal names
following the same pattern as the current default, just longer) and
measured the REAL difference against the loopback baseline from
Decision 14/15, across the 4 profiles:

| Profile | Certificate (loopback) | Certificate (realistic AWS SAN) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classical | 1.640 B | 1.876 B | **+236 B** |
| PQC | 10.878 B | 11.114 B | **+236 B** |
| Hybrid-v8 | 8.552 B | 8.786 B | **+234 B** |
| Hybrid-AND | 12.177 B | 12.649 B | **+472 B** (2x the delta of 1 chain -- both chains carry the same SAN) |

Confirmed that ServerHello/EncryptedExtensions/CertificateVerify/
Finished stayed EXACTLY the same size across both rounds -- these four
never carry any name at all. **Correction after Luciano's review:
"0B outside the Certificate" was wrong for the ClientHello -- it
carries the SNI, and my proxy today fixes `ServerName: "mtls"` (4
characters) REGARDLESS of the real destination (the same convention
the real `tls_kem_proxy` already uses, deliberately, to keep the
lab's ClientHello comparable -- see the original comment in
`tls_kem_proxy/main.go`). In a real campaign, the SNI would carry the
server's real name, not "mtls".**

**ClientHello, calculated with a name of length equivalent to the real
one:**

| Name (example) | Length | Delta vs. `"mtls"` (4 chars.) |
|---|---|---|
| EC2 private DNS (`ip-10-0-1-134.sa-east-1.compute.internal`) | 40 chars. | **+36 B** |
| EC2 public DNS (`ec2-18-230-105-42.sa-east-1.compute.amazonaws.com`) | 49 chars. | **+45 B** |

The SNI extension has only ONE variable-length field (the hostname
itself); the rest of the extension (type, lengths) is fixed, so the
delta in the ClientHello is exactly `len(real_name) - 4`, with no need
to reconstruct the whole message to confirm it. A campaign inside the
same VPC typically uses the PRIVATE DNS between instances -- **central
estimate: +36 B**; **proposed tolerance: ±15 B** (covers variation
across AWS region codes of different length, e.g. `sa-east-1`
(9 chars.) vs `ap-southeast-2` (14 chars.), plus 1-3 extra digits per
octet of the IP embedded in the name -- it does not cover the
difference between private and public DNS, which is structural, not
noise: **if the real campaign uses PUBLIC DNS instead of private, the
central estimate changes to +45B, it is not just a tolerance
question** -- recorded for Luciano to decide which DNS the real
campaign will use, before the pilot.

**New deployment-dependent field found, verified in Go's source code:
`CertificateRequest` carries
`certificate_authorities` (a list of each CA's Subject DN in
`ClientCAs`, `handshake_server_tls13.go:862`,
`certReq.certificateAuthorities = c.config.ClientCAs.Subjects()`) --
structurally deployment-dependent (it could vary if the CA's name
changed by environment). **For v9 specifically, 0B tolerance STILL
holds here** because the generator (`certs/main.go`) uses a FIXED
`CommonName` for the CA ("classico_ca" etc.), hardcoded in the code,
not parametrized by `-server-dns`/`-server-ips` nor by environment --
confirmed by reading the generator, not assumed. If the CA ever gets a
deployment-dependent name (e.g., including the region), this field
would need tolerance too; today it does not.

**No other field found with deployment dependency.** SAN IPs (present
both in the certificate and in principle relevant here) do NOT
contribute additional variability: an IP SAN is encoded as a FIXED-size
OCTET STRING per address family (4B IPv4, 16B IPv6), never as text --
swapping `127.0.0.1`/`::1` (1 IPv4 + 1 IPv6) for 2 real IPv4 addresses
was already INCLUDED in my earlier measurement of the `Certificate`

| Message | Deployment-dependent? | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| ClientHello | Yes (SNI) | **±15 B** around +36B (private DNS) -- recalculate the central estimate if the campaign uses public DNS |
| ServerHello | No | 0 B |
| EncryptedExtensions | No | 0 B |
| CertificateRequest | Structurally yes, in practice no (fixed-name CA in v9's generator) | 0 B |
| Certificate (server) | Yes (SAN) | **±50 B** around the measured delta (+236/+234/+472B per profile) |
| CertificateVerify | No | 0 B |
| Finished | No | 0 B |
| Certificate (client) | No (client identity is fixed, "opin-client-one", not tied to physical deployment) | 0 B |

**(f) Residue formula, with its components, each one's origin, and the
guard for routes with a small Δ:**

```
route_residue = (Δ_observed_latency - Σ Δ_measured_components) / Δ_observed_latency
```

**Criterion, with the requested guard:**

```
valid if: |absolute_residue| <= max(0.10 * |Δ_observed|, half_width_CI95(Δ_observed))
```

Without the guard, a route where the observed Δ between two profiles
is small (e.g., 0ms, where the Classical-PQC difference might be just
a few ms) would turn the 10%-relative criterion into an absurdly tight
threshold (10% of a small number is an even smaller number, smaller
than the measurement's own noise) -- rejecting as "high residue" a
route where, in reality, there is not enough data to distinguish
residue from noise. The guard accepts the route even with
`|residue| > 10%` IF that absolute residue is smaller than the
measurement's own statistical uncertainty -- that is, smaller than
what the 30 runs' natural noise would already explain by itself.

**Confidence-interval method: percentile bootstrap, B=10.000
resamples, over the 30 runs of each profile/route.** For each
route: (1) compute `Δ_observed` = difference of means (or medians, to
be decided based on the real distribution's shape -- this thesis has
already documented bimodality in at least one real incident, v8's
Decision 98/99, so the mean-vs-median choice is not trivial and should
be decided by looking at the real data before the pilot, not assumed
here); (2) resample with replacement the 30 runs of EACH profile,
B=10.000 times, recomputing `Δ` on each resample; (3) `half_width_CI95`
= (97.5th percentile - 2.5th percentile of the 10.000 resamples) / 2.
Bootstrap (non-parametric) chosen specifically because of this
already-documented bimodality -- a CI based on assumed normality would
be the wrong method for a distribution the thesis itself has already
shown is not normal in some cases.

| Component (Δ between profiles) | Origin/decision that measures it |
|---|---|
| Δ handshake bytes x transmission time (not extra RTT -- Decision 14 already rules out extra RTT under initcwnd=10) | Decision 14/15 (per-message table, real bytes per profile) |
| Δ sign/verify CPU (RSA-2048, ML-DSA-65) | `bench` (Decision 14) |
| Δ KEX CPU (ECDH P-384, ML-KEM-1024) | `bench` (Decision 14) |
| Δ session-ticket cost, IF on (does not apply to v9's default, tickets off -- Decision 13) | Decision 14 (diagnostic mode) |
| Δ HTTP processing time per call (access log's durationMs) | T6b (Decision 17/18), gateway's `access log` |
| Δ full-flow fixed network time (RTT x the flow's REAL number of round trips, not just the handshake's -- 44 calls, not 1) | TO BE MEASURED in the pilot -- does not exist locally yet, the full flow only runs at 0ms |

**Not closed here:** the first 2 groups (handshake+CPU) have a local
number; the last one (full-flow network, 44 real calls) only exists
with real latency, it requires the pilot. The formula and the
criterion are pre-registered; the reckoning itself cannot be closed in
local Phase 1.

**(g) Pilot and official campaign, explicitly separated, with N,
routes, and each one's estimated time -- and the corrected size
factor:**

L325, `us-east-1` L0/L14, `ap-northeast-1` L0/L30 -- see Decision 21,
point 2, for the full reconciliation). 4 profiles x **8 routes** x
N=30 = **960 combined runs -- exactly Luciano's number**,
not the 720 I had calculated with the wrong route list.

**Pilot, SMALLER, aimed at validation/calibration, not statistical
power, routes corrected to use v8's REAL names:**

| Item | Pilot | Official campaign |
|---|---|---|
| Profiles | 4 (Classical, PQC, Hybrid-v8, Hybrid-AND **strict**) | the same 4 |
| Routes | **3**: `sa-east-1/L0` (control), `sa-east-1/L219` (middle), `sa-east-1/L325` (the most distant across all of v8) | the full **8** |
| N per profile/route | **5** | 30 |
| Combined runs | 4 x 3 x 5 = **60** | 4 x 8 x 30 = **960** |

**What the pilot needs to prove, explicitly, before authorizing the
campaign (each one is a go/no-go criterion, not just a collection):**
1. **Per-message sizes** meet item (e)'s tolerance -- needs
   1 complete capture (pcap+keylog) per profile per route, not all 5
   runs instrumented this way (3 routes x 4 profiles = 12
   captures, reusing Decision 14's mechanism).
2. **The instances' real initcwnd** confirmed (`ss --info` or
   equivalent) -- once per instance TYPE used (server, client),
   not per run.
3. **Distant routes work without error** -- 0 errors across the 5
   runs of each profile on the `sa-east-1/L325` route specifically
   (325ms, the most demanding across all of v8).
4. **Counts (44/6/28/4/4) reproduce outside localhost**, under real

## 21. Interoperability matrix v2 (configuration separated from measurement), v8's 8 real routes reconciled (960 confirmed, 6 was wrong), client SAN confirmed fixed, 5 pilot criteria with numeric thresholds

**1. Matrix v2, "interoperability configuration" -- shared CA
(RSA-2048 and ML-DSA-65, one of each, used by ALL 6 modes),
all 3 KEX groups offered on both sides, never used for
measurement (only for this test).** Built from scratch in
`thesis/results/v9/integration/interop/` (new, single process,
certificates generated in memory, nothing on disk). A methodological
finding along the way: the first version had the server AND the
client read with the SAME 2s deadline after the handshake -- a race
(whoever closed first decided the result), which made even
strict-against-strict (which must succeed) fail by luck half the
time. Fixed by having the server WRITE a confirmation byte instead of
reading -- no race, identical result across 3 repeated rounds.

| Classical | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | `handshake failure` -- no Dual | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| Classical | Hybrid-AND non-strict | SUCCESS | group=SecP384r1MLKEM1024, Dual not used | RSA | RSA | false | no |
| PQC | Classical | SUCCESS | group=SecP384r1MLKEM1024 | RSA | ML-DSA | false | no |
| PQC | PQC | SUCCESS | group=SecP384r1MLKEM1024 | ML-DSA | ML-DSA | false | no |
| PQC | Hybrid-v8 | FAILURE | `bad certificate` -- missing AltSignatureValue | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| PQC | Hybrid-AND strict | FAILURE | `handshake failure` -- no Dual | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| PQC | Hybrid-AND non-strict | SUCCESS | group=SecP384r1MLKEM1024, Dual not used | RSA | ML-DSA | false | no |

| Hybrid-AND non-strict | PQC | SUCCESS | group=SecP384r1MLKEM1024, Dual not used | ML-DSA | RSA | false | no |

**Explicitly requested records:**

1. **Every client in this configuration offered every signature
   scheme, including ML-DSA-65** -- no config in this matrix (neither
   before nor now) explicitly sets `Config.SignatureSchemes`, in any
   mode; this toolchain's Go announces the complete DEFAULT list in
   the ClientHello's `signature_algorithms`, which already includes
   ML-DSA-65 natively (confirmed indirectly: the PQC/Hybrid-v8/
   Hybrid-AND profiles only work because this signature is in the
   default, it never needed an explicit opt-in in either harness).
   The Dual scheme (`0xFE65`) is the ONLY one that ONLY appears when
   `Config.Dual` is actually configured -- that one really is an
   opt-in, not the default.
2. **The Hybrid-v8 server's X.509 gate refuses any client without
   `AltSignatureValue`, ALWAYS, regardless of who the client is** --
   confirmed in the 2 rows `Classical -> Hybrid-v8` and `PQC ->
   Hybrid-v8`, both `FAILURE`, the exact same error (`bad certificate --
   missing AltSignatureValue`), despite Classical and PQC being
   completely different identities (RSA vs. pure ML-DSA) -- the gate
   does not distinguish WHO is missing the extension, only that it is
   missing. **Additional finding, not requested but relevant:** this
   gate is ASYMMETRIC -- only the Hybrid-v8 SERVER verifies (via
   `VerifyPeerCertificate`); no CLIENT in this matrix, including
   Hybrid-v8 itself acting as a client, verifies the server side's
   alternative signature. A "fake" Hybrid-v8 server (valid RSA, no
   AltSignatureValue) would fool a Hybrid-v8 client without being
   detected -- recorded here, not fixed (outside this round's
   request).

**Positive finding regarding SAD §3.4 (classical and migrated clients
DO COMMUNICATE, when the configuration allows it):** Classical<->PQC
succeeds in both directions -- each side presents its own certificate
type (RSA or ML-DSA), verified by the other side's SHARED trust pool.
Hybrid-v8 interoperates with ALL 4 other modes except strict
Hybrid-AND (its own X.509 gate is a protection INDEPENDENT of the TLS
Dual -- it rejects pure Classical/PQC the same way Dual would, but via
a different mechanism, not interoperable with Dual).

**2. PKI procedure, corrected -- ONE issuance, not one per instance.**

The previous version was wrong: "each instance generates its own PKI"
would produce DIFFERENT CAs on each side, breaking mutual verification
(exactly the kind of error this same folder's Decision 17 had already
fixed in the local harness -- it should not have come back in the
pilot's procedure). Corrected:

1. The server comes up first, Terraform resolves its real address
   (IP/DNS). ONLY AFTER this, **a single call** to the generator
   (`certs/main.go`, the same already-existing binary, no change) with
   `-server-dns=<real hostname>` `-server-ips=<real IP>`
   `-client-dns=opin-client-one`, running on the OPERATOR's machine
   (inside this session, local scratch) or on an ephemeral control
   instance -- never directly on the server/client instances,
   because neither knows the OTHER's address at its own boot time.
   This call produces, all at once: 1 CA + 1 server + 1 client PER
   profile (4 profiles), all with the SAME server/client identity,
   signed by CAs SHARED between both sides -- exactly what needed
   fixing.
2. **Distribution, via `scp` over the operator's SAME SSH channel**
   (already in use since v8 -- `MOCKOPIN_OPERATOR_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE`,
   control IP never printed): the server receives the 4 SERVER
   certificates+keys + the public CAs (to validate the clients); the
   client receives the 4 CLIENT certificates+keys + the SAME public
   CAs (to validate the server). `scp`, not SSM Parameter Store --
   simpler, does not put the private key into YET ANOTHER system (SSM
   would store the key as a SecureString, but it is an extra system
   with its own attack surface; `scp` over a channel that already
   exists adds nothing new to protect).
3. **Cleanup:** the operator's LOCAL copy (this session's scratch) is
   deleted immediately after successful delivery is confirmed on both
   instances (checksum or simply re-reading the remote file). The copy
   on EACH instance is deleted at the end of that instance's use --
   for the client, at the end of its last run before switching
   route/region (or being destroyed); for the server, at the end of
   the entire pilot. No key is ever logged in clear text at any point
   (not in the `scp` transport, which is encrypted by nature, nor in
   any shell log).

**3. Destruction procedure, corrected -- verification by TAG, not
just by resource type, plus auto-shutdown with a defined N.**

- **Tag-based verification, a single API call:** `aws
  resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters
  Key=Project,Values=mockopin-pqc-v9` before AND after each destroy --
  covers EVERYTHING that accepts a tag in a single call (instances,
  EBS volumes, network interfaces, security groups, key pairs, elastic
  IPs), unlike the real v8, which verified type by type
  (`describe-instances`/
  `describe-security-groups`/`describe-key-pairs`/`describe-volumes`)
  and never specifically checked network interfaces (confirmed by
  searching `v8/DECISIONS.md` -- no hit for
  `describe-network-interfaces` nor for this tags API). Expected to be
  **empty** after each destroy; any non-empty result blocks ending the
  session.
- **Auto-shutdown, reusing v8's REAL module** (not reinvented --
  `modules/campaign_instance/templates/
  safety_timer.sh.tftpl`, already tested, already in production
  there): same mechanism (systemd timer, checks a deadline file every
  5min), **N = 4 hours** for the pilot (not v8's default 48h, which is
  meant for a multi-day CAMPAIGN) -- a generous margin over the
  pilot's 1-1.5h estimate (Decision 20), but short enough to not leave
  anything running all night if the session drops. Auto-shuts-down
  (does not destroy) -- the tag-based verification above is what
  confirms real destruction, the timer is just the safety net against
  forgetting.

**4. 7-criteria evaluator -- written and tested against real local
data, 3 bugs found and fixed along the way.**

`thesis/results/v9/integration/evaluate_criteria.py` (new) -- reads
the artifacts `run_t6.sh` and a T6b run already produce (no new
format invented) and computes criteria 1, 4, 5, and 6 (the ones
Luciano confirmed are locally assessable); 2, 3, and 7 have the logic
written but return `None` (no data) until real pilot artifacts exist.

**Three real bugs found testing against a real `run_t6.sh` run + a
real T6b run (not invented data):**
1. The per-profile block slicing stopped at the first `==` it found
   (including ones inside the block itself, such as "==
   gateway" or "== tshark: records..."), never reaching the
   per-message size section. Fixed: slicing goes until the NEXT `==
   Profile:`, not until any `==`.
2. The error check (`FATAL:`) was capturing the Dockerfile's OWN text
   (`echo "FATAL: ..." >&2; exit 1; }`), which Docker reprints as a
   normal part of the build log even on a successful build --
   reporting a false positive on a round that actually passed. Fixed:
   only a `FATAL:` line that does NOT have shell syntax (`>&2`/
   `exit 1`) alongside it counts as a real error.
3. The `Certificate` message size was being summed counting the
   SERVER's and the CLIENT's together (both have the same TLS type,
   11) -- nearly doubling the number. Fixed: only count the
   `Certificate` from the frame that ALSO contains `ServerHello`
   (type 2), which is unambiguously the server's flight.

**Result, running against a real run of the local harness (4
profiles, `run_t6.sh` + a real T6b run of the Classical profile):**

```
criterio 1 (sizes per message): PASS
criterio 2 (real initcwnd): N/A (no data -- needs the pilot)
criterio 3 (zero errors on the farthest route): N/A (no data -- needs the pilot)
criterio 4 (flow counts): PASS
criterio 5 (zero errors): PASS
criterio 6 (complete instrumentation + assertions): PASS
criterio 7 (per-route latency sanity): N/A (no data -- needs the pilot)
```

**5. Go binary -- SHA-256 calculated, reproducibility confirmed.**

```
gateway: fa4c9c32412abab4533bb40e8a45524c149be59e7d10888b00a1895bc0dc4871
proxy:   a4f901a94253aa6bafaf0579518f9487405e3358218db5a9e635d13d55c1d6e9
```

Confirmed reproducible: a full rebuild with `--no-cache` (identical
source, identical toolchain) produced the SAME `gateway` hash, byte
for byte, not just "similar." **Procedure proposed for the pilot:**
build ONCE (in this session or on an ephemeral control instance),
compute the SHA-256, `scp` the binary (not the source code, do not
rebuild on each instance) to the server and to the client along with
a `.sha256` file, and each instance runs `sha256sum -c` at boot before
using the binary -- fails that instance's deployment if the hash does
not match, instead of running a potentially different binary without
knowing it.

**6. Hybrid-v8, limitation recorded -- kept as is, for fidelity to
v8.** Explicitly confirmed (Decision 21, extra finding, now formalized
as a documented profile limitation): **no client in this matrix --
including Hybrid-v8 itself acting as a client -- verifies the SERVER
certificate's alternative signature (`AltSignatureValue`); only the
server verifies the client's.** This is faithful to the real v8's
behavior, not a gap introduced by v9: the real `tls_kem_proxy` uses
`InsecureSkipVerify: true` (performs NO server chain verification at
all, neither classical nor alternative); v9 is already stricter than
that (always verifies the server's classical RSA chain, Decision 12),
it just does not extend that verification to the alternative X.509
gate. **Measurement implication, recorded:** the CLIENT's CPU cost in
the Hybrid-v8 profile (bench, Decision 14) UNDERESTIMATES the real
cost of a client that actually verified the server's alternative
signature -- this operation (1 extra ML-DSA-65 verification per
connection) is never exercised on the client side, neither in v8 nor
in v9. **Decision: kept as is**, for fidelity to v8 -- recorded here
so whoever reads Hybrid-v8's CPU numbers knows the client side
specifically has this downward bias, it is not a "complete" number.

Same rules: no action on AWS, no commit before the scanner, report in
chat.

## 23. Six corrections to T8/procedure/evaluator -- local PKI only deleted at the end of the pilot, run order by profile block (replicating the real v8), MongoDB/Node verified by real digest (not by label), criterion 1 confirmed at message level + MSS/MTU/snaplen in the pilot, auto-shutdown fixed to terminate, HTTP sizes compared byte for byte in a real run

**1. PKI, operator's local copy -- fixed: only deleted at the END of
the pilot, not after the first confirmed delivery.**

The previous version (Decision 22, item 2.3) was wrong for the same
reason Luciano himself pointed out: the pilot has **3 clients**
(L0, L219, L325), not 1 -- and all 3 exist and operate
**simultaneously** during the pilot (see point 2 below: a profile
block needs all 3 routes available at the same time for the
round-robin). Deleting the local copy after "delivery confirmation"
sounds safe, but does not clearly define after delivery to WHICH of
the 3 clients -- and if a client needs to be replaced mid-pilot
(crash, instance recreated), reissuing the PKI from scratch would
change the CA, invalidating the trust already established with the
server and with the other 2 clients still standing. **Fixed:** the
operator's local copy (this session's scratch) is retained until the
entire pilot ends -- it is only deleted after the LAST destroy
(server + 3 clients) is confirmed. The copy on EACH instance keeps
being deleted at the end of THAT instance's use (same as Decision 22
already said -- this part did not change, only the OPERATOR's copy).

**2. Run order -- fixed to randomization per profile BLOCK, fixed
round-robin route within the block, replicating the real v8.**

Decision 22's proposal ("profile randomized per run") was wrong: every
profile switch requires restarting the `gateway`/`proxy` (new TLS
config -- curve group, CA, Dual), and that restart's readiness probe
(the same one that caused the "7th connection," Decision 18) would
fall INSIDE the measured window if the profile changed every run.
Checked how the real v8 actually ordered things
(`switch_crypto_profile.py` is the campaign's real orchestrator,
looked up directly, not from memory): **profile drawn once PER
WINDOW** (the real v8 has 3 windows/day, each with its own drawn
order); **within a window, the ROUTE is never drawn** -- fixed
round-robin (`L0, L14, L30, ...`, always the same literal order),
repeated run after run. In other words: v8 switches profile
(restarts the gateway) ONCE, does the warm-up (5 discards,
`SETTLING_WARMUP_RUNS`), and only AFTER THAT walks through the routes
in a fixed round-robin, several times, before switching to the next
drawn profile.

**Adopted for v9's pilot, under the same logic:** since the pilot
probably fits in a single window (Decision 20), the order of the 4
profiles is drawn **once, for the entire pilot**; within each profile
block, the round-robin walks through the pilot's 3 routes (`L0,
L219, L325`, fixed order) **N=5 times each** = 15 runs per
profile, 60 in total. The `gateway`/`proxy` only restarts on a block
SWITCH (4 times in total, not 60) -- each restart's readiness probe
stays outside the measured window, exactly as intended.
**Direct consequence for point 1:** since the round-robin needs all
3 routes (3 client instances) available at the same time throughout
an ENTIRE profile block, the 3 clients need to be up and with the PKI
already delivered BEFORE the first block begins -- reinforcing why
the operator's copy cannot be deleted right after the "first"
delivery.

**3. MongoDB and Node.js -- fixed: verified by real digest, not by a
matching label on both ends.**

Decision 22 marked "SAME, confirmed" just because the label
`mongo:latest`/`node:24-alpine` appeared on both ends -- exactly the
error Luciano pointed out. I re-verified directly against the source,
by digest:

| Image | Where it is pinned | Real digest | Confirmed real version (`--version` inside the container) |
|---|---|---|---|
| MongoDB (insurance-server-lambdas) | `insurance-server-lambdas/docker-compose.yml:324` | `sha256:dc28ed5a9d0fc616903c3f463bb1e53b92b49f441721b91926e87d90bf957ce8` (note: an earlier transcription of mine, only in working text, had a 1-digit error in this hash -- `f469bb` instead of the real `f463bb`; it never made it into this file, but recorded here so it is not repeated) | `db version v9.0.4`, `gitVersion 64ade602b836c9adeffba7fa038c887ffab56196`, `openSSLVersion OpenSSL 3.5.5` |
| Node (mock_as) | `mock-service-os/mock_as/Dockerfile:1` | `sha256:44fce696f38ba8c987c4db89954051000bbd05ffd8d8659ba15ed4a8602e937f` | `v24.22.0` |

Both files (`insurance-server-lambdas/docker-compose.yml` and
`mock-service-os/mock_as/Dockerfile`) **were never touched by any v9
commit** (confirmed via `git log -- <file>`, the last commit on each
one predates v9's existence) -- T6b reuses both WITH NO CHANGE, so
v8 (the real campaign) and v9 (local T6b, and the pilot afterward)
literally run the SAME file, SAME digest. This is why **"SAME" is
correct here** -- but now confirmed by digest + a real version that
was actually run, not assumed from the label.

**Illustration of why a label alone is unsafe** (a finding along the
way, recorded as context, not as a v8-vs-v9 divergence): there is a
THIRD `node:24-alpine` image in the repo,
`thesis/scripts/pqc-signer/Dockerfile:12`, pinned by a DIFFERENT
digest
(`sha256:d32cdf619f63fe0471182d08996dd516c6275bb5fd31ae06e55a570bd9e1ad43`),
which resolves to a different REAL version (`v24.19.0`, not `v24.22.0`)
-- the same literal label `node:24-alpine`, pinned at different
times, points to genuinely different Node builds. This file was also
never touched by v9 (last commit
`055ffa81`/`388e874c`, both pre-v9) -- so it too is "same" v8 vs. v9
by construction, it just serves as concrete proof that the digest
check was necessary, not perfectionism.

**4. Criterion 1 and MTU -- confirmed at message level (not packet);
real MSS/path MTU and the initcwnd x MSS check added to the pilot;
the pilot's snaplen cannot reuse the real v8's 256.**

Confirmed by reading `measure/measure.sh` directly (lines 52-55): the
section `evaluate_criteria.py` uses for criterion 1 comes from
`tshark -r
"$PCAP" -o "tls.keylog_file: $KEYLOG" -Y tls.handshake -T fields -e
tls.handshake.type -e tls.handshake.length` -- `tls.handshake.length`
is the length field DECLARED INSIDE the TLS message itself (after
decryption and TCP reassembly done by tshark via the keylog), not the
size of a packet/frame. Packet size (`tcp.len`) only appears in a
SEPARATE section, explicitly labeled "cross-check" (line 57-58), never
used by criterion 1. Confirms what Decision 20 had already assumed,
now read in the source, not remembered.

The local capture (`measure.sh` line 19) already uses `tcpdump -i lo -s 0`
(full snaplen, no truncation) -- but v8's REAL campaign uses
`TCPDUMP_SNAPLEN_BYTES` = **256**, confirmed in
`v8/campaign/scripts/campaign_run.py` (lines 1686/2464) and in
`v8/campaign/README.md` itself ("Pcap capture: snaplen 256, handshake
measured two ways", v8's Decision 79) -- sufficient there because
v8's only use of the pcap was confirming SNI visibility/tolerance in
the ClientHello (near the start of the record). **This is NOT
sufficient for v9's pilot:** the `Certificate` messages of the
PQC/Hybrid-AND profiles measure 5.632B/6.582B (Decision 15/20) -- a
256 snaplen would irrecoverably truncate the message's content (bytes
lost, not just deferred), breaking tshark's reassembly well before the
record's end. **Recorded in the pilot's procedure: the capture uses
`tcpdump -s 0` (or a snaplen explicitly larger than the largest
expected message, with margin), never the real v8 campaign's
conventional 256.**

**New pilot items, added to the checklist:**
- Record the real MSS and the real path MTU on each of the pilot's 3
  routes (e.g., `tracepath <destination>` from each client instance to
  the server, or `ip route get`/`ss --info` after a real connection
  for the negotiated MSS).
- Verify that the server's FIRST flight (ServerHello +
  EncryptedExtensions + CertificateRequest + Certificate +
  CertificateVerify + Finished, Decision 15) fits within
  `initcwnd x MSS` -- if it does not fit, criterion 2 (real initcwnd)
  and the very assumption of "no extra RTT in the handshake" (Decision
  14/22) need to be revisited before accepting the pilot's numbers.

**5. Auto-shutdown -- confirmed/fixed: `terminate`, not just
`stop`.**

Confirmed directly in the real module
(`v8/campaign/terraform/modules/campaign_instance/main.tf`): the
`resource "aws_instance" "this"` NEVER sets
`instance_initiated_shutdown_behavior` -- it stays at AWS's default,
which is `"stop"` (confirmed by absence: no hit for
`shutdown_behavior` in this file). This means the real v8's
`safety_timer.sh.tftpl`, when it triggers a `shutdown` inside the
guest after the deadline, only STOPS the instance -- it keeps
existing (and can be billed for EBS/elastic IP) until someone actually
destroys it. **For v9's pilot, a deliberate divergence, recorded: the
Terraform module (when written, reusing `campaign_instance` as a
base) explicitly sets
`instance_initiated_shutdown_behavior = "terminate"`** -- the safety
auto-shutdown (Decision 22, N=4h) really TERMINATES the instance, not
just stops it, reducing the residual-cost window should the session
drop without a manual teardown.

**6. HTTP body/header sizes -- compared byte for byte in a real run,
no longer "by construction" without measuring.**

Decision 22 (the "HTTP body and header sizes" item) had honestly
recorded the gap: the comparison had never been run. I ran it now: I
used v8's real data already collected in
`thesis/results/v8/janela1/experiment1 - Classic/sa-east-1/L0/runs/
w01_run01.calls.jsonl` (44 calls, Classical profile, L0 route) as a
reference, and brought up a fresh v9 T6b round (this session's
`gateway`/`proxy` containers, `classico` profile, against the SAME
real backend `auth`/`mockapi`/`mongodb`/`localstack` that was already
up, unmodified) via a minimal driver that calls
`run_insurance_flow`/`run_person_flow` from `opin_flow.py` itself
directly (same production code, no new flag) and dumps the resulting
44 calls. I compared them pair by pair, in the same order (same
endpoint sequence in both rounds, confirming identical count and
order again):

- **`request_bytes` (body + headers of each REQUEST): 44/44 identical,
  byte for byte, with no exception.**
- **`response_bytes`: 14/44 identical byte for byte** (endpoints with
  deterministic content -- initial JWKS, CA, token issuance,
  `/auth`, `/request`, login/consent-redirect confirmations).
- **30/44 differ by exactly 1 byte**, always in the same pattern:
  confined to endpoints whose response body embeds (a) `mock_as`'s own
  JWKS, derived from an EPHEMERAL RSA-2048 key generated at runtime
  (the modulus `n`'s big-integer serialization can legitimately vary
  ±1 byte between two distinct key generations, depending on the high
  bits of the drawn modulus -- this is expected per-run key noise, not
  a bug), or (b) business data randomly generated by
  `insurance-server-lambdas` itself (claim/premium values) on every
  run -- a generator never altered by v9 (confirmed via
  `git log`). This same noise source (±1 byte, sometimes more on
  monetary values) exists running v8 twice in a row against itself,
  it is not a v8-vs-v9 divergence. **Honest caveat:** I did not open
  the raw body of each response byte by byte to point at the exact
  character that differs in each of the 30 cases -- the pattern
  (exactly 1-byte difference, confined to endpoints with content
  known to be random per run, zero difference everywhere else) is
  strong evidence, not a byte-for-byte proof case by case.

**Result recorded in the checklist (corrects Decision 22's "HTTP body
and header sizes" row):** from "SAME by construction,
NOT compared" to **"SAME, now measured: requests 44/44 exact;
responses 14/44 exact and 30/44 with a known ±1-byte random noise
(ephemeral key/mock data), the same pattern already expected within
v8 itself, run to run"**.

Same rules: no action on AWS, no commit before the scanner, report in
chat.

## 24. Correction of Decision 23 item 6's explanation (the "random noise" hypothesis was WRONG -- the real cause identified and proven: a calendar artifact in the RS's Date header); capture kept separate from the timed measurement, with a scheme for the pilot and for the campaign; per-block collection with hashing; terminate confirmed; estimated cost of the pilot and of the official campaign with margin

**1. HTTP SIZES -- Decision 23's explanation was wrong. Proof by
replay, not accepted by hypothesis.**

Luciano asked for exactly the missing proof: compare `w01_run01`
with `w01_run02` from v8 ITSELF (same execution window, same
container boot). Result: **0/44 calls differ between the two real v8
runs.** This directly refutes Decision 23's "per-run random noise"
hypothesis (ephemeral key regenerated on every run, random mock
data) -- if it were genuine per-run noise, it would ALSO show up
within v8 itself, run to run, and it does not.

Additional investigation, isolating the real variable:
1. I brought up the REAL `mtls` (unmodified) + the REAL
   `tls_kem_proxy` (precompiled image) in this session, and ran the
   SAME `opin_flow.py` (production code, no new flag) against them,
   today -- 44 calls captured (`v8real`).
2. I compared `v8real` (today) against v9 (today, this session's
   containers): **0/44 differ.** v8 and v9 are byte-identical TODAY,
   across all 44 calls.
3. I compared `v8real` (today) against the archived file `w01_run01`
   (2026-10-30): **18/44 differ, each by exactly 1 byte** --
   all and ONLY the calls served by the Resource Server
   (`mockapi`/`insurance-server-lambdas`, Java/Micronaut): the RS's
   `/jwks`, `/consents` (POST and GET), `/insurance-person/*`. No AS
   call (`mock_as`/oidc-provider, Node) appears in that list.

**Root cause, identified and confirmed, not assumed:** I captured the
raw body of the RS's `/jwks` response (the call with an Authorization
Bearer, index 4) -- exactly 455 bytes, matching the real static key
(`insurance-server-lambdas/src/main/resources/crypto-profiles/
classic.json`, committed, never regenerated, `kid` identical to the
archived one: `041486ea-f7b8-4b36-9dfb-fadf2966d0e8`). Fixed, 100%
deterministic body -- the 1-byte difference can only be in the
header. The `Date` header captured today (November 7th):
`"Sat, 7 Nov 2026
13:15:02 GMT"` -- **no leading zero on the day** (15 characters
before the year). The RS's (Java/Micronaut) HTTP `Date` formatter
does NOT zero-pad single-digit days (1-9), unlike the AS (Node/
oidc-provider), which always zero-pads (`"Sat, 07 Nov 2026..."`,
confirmed in call idx0, which IS from the AS and NEVER appears in the
difference list). The archived file was recorded on 2026-10-30 --
**day 30, two digits, with no such ambiguity.** Today is day 7 -- one
digit, 1 byte shorter in the `Date` header, on exactly every call that
passes through the RS.

**This is NOT noise: it is a DETERMINISTIC artifact, explained and
tied to the CALENDAR date on which the comparison is made**, not to
v8 vs. v9 (confirmed: v8real-today vs. v9-today = 0/44 differences)
and not to run-to-run variation (confirmed: v8 run01 vs. run02 =
0/44). It reappears whenever one side of the comparison was captured
on a single-digit day (1-9 of any month) and the other side on a
two-digit day -- and it disappears (becomes 0/44) when both sides
have the same digit count in the day, as happened in both
"today vs. today" tests above. **Corrects Decision 23: the "ephemeral
key"/"random mock data" explanation was WRONG (no key is ephemeral
here -- both ends, AS and RS, load committed static keys) -- the real
cause is the RS's `Date` header formatting.** T8 checklist result
corrected again: HTTP body and header sizes are
**SAME between v8 and v9, confirmed by a double measurement
(today-vs-today, 0/44 differences); the only difference source found
is a calendar artifact of the RS itself (unrelated to v8-vs-v9), which
self-corrects outside the 1-9-day-of-the-month window.**

**2. TERMINATE AND ARTIFACTS -- per-block collection added to the
procedure, with integrity verification before proceeding.**

Correct: with `instance_initiated_shutdown_behavior = "terminate"`
(Decision 23, item 5), the root EBS volume is deleted along with the
destroy -- any artifact that only existed on the instance's disk is
lost if teardown fires before collection. Added to the procedure: at
the END of EACH of the 4 profile blocks (not just at the end of the
entire pilot), the operator copies that block's artifacts
(gateway/proxy logs, pcap+keylog from that block's captures,
`calls.jsonl` from the 15 runs) to the operator's machine via `scp`,
computes the SHA-256 of each received file and checks it against the
hash computed ON the instance before deleting the remote original --
only proceeds to the next block (or to the destroy, on the last
block) after integrity is confirmed.
**Auto-shutdown (N=4h, Decision 23) remains only the safety net
against a dropped session -- per-block collection is the primary
mechanism, it does not depend on it.**

**3. CAPTURE vs. LATENCY -- scheme defined: capture kept separate
from the timed runs, both in the pilot and in the official campaign.**

**Which runs carry capture:** the 12 from criterion 1 (4 profiles x 3
routes, Decision 20/21) -- ONE complete capture (`tcpdump -s 0` +
keylog) per profile x route cell, not all 15 runs of that block. The
pilot's 60 runs remain ALL timed (criteria 5/6/7 require this); the
capture runs on a DEDICATED, additional run, outside the statistical
count of 15 per block -- exactly replicating the pattern v7 already
used (v7's Decision 15: a packet captured by an observer `--rm`,
OUTSIDE the statistical batch, "the size batch and the latency batch
are different sets of runs").

**Perturbation measured locally (N=5 with vs. without capture,
Classical profile, same machine):** I ran v9's `gateway`+`proxy`
inside the SAME container (no local network traversal, like
`measure.sh`) 5 times WITH `tcpdump -s 0`+keylog (as the real
`measure.sh` does) and 5 times WITHOUT any capture, extracting the
`handshakeDurationUs` the `proxy` itself reports. **Without capture:**
7436, 6326, 12795, 10719,
6089 µs (mean 8673). **With capture:** 4320, 4744, 6183, 7064, 4636 µs
(mean 5389). **Honest result: the WITH-capture sample came out
SMALLER, not larger** -- the opposite of what a real perturbation
would cause. I conclude that, at this scale (microseconds, local
loopback, N=5), the environment's background variance (Docker
scheduling, container boot) completely dominates any real capture
cost -- **this local test is inconclusive, it does not prove the
capture is harmless, only that the effect (if it exists) is below the
background noise measured here.** Honestly recorded: the real test
needs to be redone in the pilot, on a route with REAL network latency
(where the handshake takes tens to hundreds of ms, not 5-13), N=5 with
vs. without capture, same route and profile -- only there is the
result conclusive.

**Scheme proposed for the official campaign (960 runs):** capture
runs ONLY on the dedicated runs (4 profiles x 8 routes... no,
3 of the 8 routes are enough for the criterion -- but if Luciano
wants all 8 routes captured, that is 32 dedicated captures, 4
profiles x 8
routes), each OUTSIDE the 30 statistical runs of that
cell -- never the same run counted twice. The 30 statistical runs per
cell (960 in total) NEVER carry `tcpdump`/keylog turned on, exactly
as v7 separated the "size batch" from the "latency
batch." This guarantees the official latency number never includes
the cost (measured or not) of running the capture.

**4. AUTO-SHUTDOWN -- reconfirmed.** `terminate`, not `stop`
(Decision 23, item 5, no change -- reconfirmed here because of
item 2 above, which depends on this semantics).

**5. COST -- estimated by arithmetic, with declared sources and
dates, with no AWS call at all.**

- Cross-region transfer: negligible at this scale (the real v8
  measured ~US$0.14 for the ENTIRE 720-run campaign) ≈ US$0.02
- **Subtotal: ≈ US$0.89. With a 30% margin: ≈ US$1.15.**

This matches real precedent already recorded in `v8/DECISIONS.md`
(several pilot attempts of similar scale/duration really cost
US$0.93, US$1.10, and US$1.80) -- the estimate is not fanciful, it
reproduces the same order of magnitude the real v8 already measured.
**Fits within US$27.72 with a large margin (uses ~4-7% of the cap).**

**v9's official campaign (960 runs, 4 profiles x 8 routes x 30 --
33% more runs than the real v8, the same 8 routes/regions, the same
instance types):** scaling the real v8 anchor (US$29.34 / 22.45h for
720 runs = 3 profiles) linearly per profile (US$9.78 and
7.48h of fleet-time per profile, per the real v8): **4 profiles -> ≈
29.9h of fleet-time, ≈ US$39.12 before margin.** **With a 30% margin:
≈ US$50.86.**
**Does NOT fit within US$27.72** -- the full official campaign, under
this estimate, is between 1.4x (no margin) and 1.8x (with margin)
above that value. If US$27.72 is meant as a cap just for the PILOT,
the pilot fits with a large margin (item above); if it is meant as
the cap for the entire OFFICIAL CAMPAIGN, this estimate indicates it
does not fit, and the decision (reduce N, reduce routes, raise the
cap, or accept the overrun) is Luciano's -- not assumed here.

Same rules: no action on AWS, no commit before the scanner, report in
chat.

## 25. Instance types reconciled (m7i-flex.large/t4g.micro confirmed in the real tfstate, not the old plan's t3.xlarge/t3.medium); cross-arch amd64+arm64 Go build with reproducible per-architecture hash; the control instance's role explained and kept; the Date artifact recorded as a limitation with day-boundary handling; regional price sensitivity and the price sources made explicit

**1. TYPES AND ARCHITECTURE -- reconciled against v8's real tfstate,
not against the old plan.**

The "t3.xlarge"/"t3.medium" Luciano read comes from a **draft plan
predating any real v8 research** (the phase plan recorded at the
start of this session, before Decision 22 researched the real v8) --
it was never written into v9's `DECISIONS.md`; v9's `DECISIONS.md`
(Decision 22 onward) has always used
`m7i-flex.large`/`t4g.micro`. I reconfirmed this now directly against
the most concrete artifact possible, not prose:
`thesis/results/v8/campaign/
terraform/terraform.tfstate.backup` (the REAL state, post-apply, not
the plan) -- `grep instance_type` shows **11 instances with
`"instance_type": "m7i-flex.large"`** (servers and clients, all
x86_64) and **1 with `"instance_type": "t4g.micro"`** (control,
arm64), matching exactly `variables.tf`
(`server_client_instance_type`, no default -- requires an explicit
choice; `control_instance_type`, default `"t4g.micro"`,
commented as "free-tier-eligible, small -- the control instance
never runs the real workload"). **Corrected the T8 "Instance types"
row (Decision 22):** from "NOT VERIFIABLE WITHOUT AWS" to
**"SAME, by decision -- verifiable and verified NOW"**, because the
TYPE is a config string, it does not depend on AWS to be specified;
only the exact resolved AMI ID (its own row, `most_recent=true`)
still depends on a real resolution.

**Cross-architecture build, each with a reproducible hash, tested
now:** I built `gateway` for the corrected toolchain (go1.27.3, the
same `mockopin-v9-toolchain` image) with `GOARCH=amd64` and with
`GOARCH=arm64` separately, and REBUILT both from scratch (new
container, same source, same toolchain) to confirm reproducibility:

```
amd64: 94bd9cadf87cc665b6fda5114b10cc3ddc771432436d0973b1cacc1630ee6537  (identical across both builds)
arm64: 458009d2a77544f7919989ce70368b6e583b997e6b74df3e12326d93c342d78a  (identical across both builds)
```

Two hashes DIFFERENT from each other (expected -- different machine
code), each stable/reproducible within its own architecture
(expected -- confirms that build reproducibility (Decision 22,
item 5) holds for both architectures, not just amd64). **Real use:**
the `gateway`/`proxy` runs on the SERVER and on the 3 CLIENTS, all
`m7i-flex.large` (amd64) -- this is the source-hash pair that needs
to be checked (`sha256sum -c`) on EACH of these 4 instances before
using the binary. **The CONTROL instance (arm64) does not run
`gateway`/`proxy` in the current design** (it only orchestrates via
SSH, Section 2 below) -- the arm64 build is prepared anyway, by
explicit request and as a precaution (it lets the control instance
run a connectivity self-test with the SAME binary, independent of the
real x86 path, if Luciano wants this extra diagnostic before each
block) -- but, honestly, it is not used by today's measured flow.
**Hash checking is always architecture-aware**: each
instance checks against the hash FOR ITS OWN architecture (amd64 on
the 4 `m7i-flex.large`, arm64 on the control instance if it ever runs
the binary), never crossed -- comparing an amd64 hash against an
arm64 binary
would always fail, by design (they are different files).

**Burstable CPU risk (`t4g.micro`) -- assessed, low impact on the
measured/captured path, but monitoring proposed as a precaution.**
`t4g.micro` is from the T family (Graviton2, burstable): low baseline
performance, with a CPU credit that accumulates when idle and
depletes under sustained load -- under exhaustion, the instance is
throttled below baseline. `m7i-flex.large` (the server and the 3
clients -- where the timed HTTP flow and the `tcpdump -s 0`/keylog
ACTUALLY run) is from the M "Flex" family: a higher baseline, WITHOUT
the depleting credit mechanism -- it does not suffer the same risk.
**Conclusion: the instance at risk of credit-based throttling is
EXACTLY the one that runs neither the timed flow nor the capture**
(the control instance only does SSH/orchestration) -- the risk does
not directly contaminate the measured data. **But it could delay the
round-robin's cadence** (Decision 23, item 2) if the control instance
slows down under credit exhaustion, creating time gaps between runs
(not a bias in the numbers, which are self-contained client-side,
just possibly a delay/a window longer than planned).
**Monitoring proposed, added to the procedure:** before and after
EACH profile block (4 times in the pilot), run `ethtool -S` does not
apply here -- the real mechanism is `aws cloudwatch get-metric-
statistics --metric-name CPUCreditBalance` (outside this session's
reach, "no AWS") OR, inside the instance itself, check `/proc/stat`/
perceived load before/after as a cheap proxy; the formal item remains
part of the pilot's procedure (not executable without AWS now), with
the criterion: the control instance's credit balance cannot reach
zero during the pilot -- if it does, document the observed delay in
cadence, do not discard the data (which remains valid, just
potentially more spread out in time).

**2. CONTROL -- role explained (same as the real v8), kept in the
procedure.**

I looked up the exact role directly in `v8/DECISIONS.md`, Decision 49
("Campaign control-plane infrastructure"), instead of assuming.
**What the control instance DOES in the real v8, and will do
identically in v9:** it is the ORCHESTRATOR -- runs the campaign
script (equivalent to the real `campaign_run.py`) under `systemd`,
holds the campaign's exclusive SSH key (generated by Terraform, never
written into the repository) and uses THAT key to connect to the
server and to the clients, never the other way around; it is what
decides the ORDER (drawn profile, route round-robin -- exactly the
mechanism Decision 23, item 2, relies on something orchestrating) and
fires each run via SSH. **What the control instance DOES NOT DO,
confirmed in the same decision:** it has no AWS credential or role of
its own (`iam_instance_profile` never set -- it cannot do `terraform
destroy` nor any AWS call on its own); it does not run the measured
HTTP flow nor the capture (that is on the server/clients). Inbound
SSH to the server/clients only accepts connections from the CONTROL
instance's own elastic IP (never the operator directly) -- the
operator talks only to the control instance, and the control instance
talks to the rest. **Decision: kept in v9's procedure, identical in
role** -- without it, there would be nothing to fire the round-robin
across the 3 clients in the right order nor anything to hold/relay
the campaign key; it is also where the operational copy of the PKI
can be mirrored (besides the operator's copy, Decision 23 item 1) if
Luciano wants a second copy inside the campaign's network.

**3. DATE -- recorded as a known limitation in the checklist, with a
day-boundary handling proposed.**

Added to T8's checklist (Decision 22) and to the pilot's limitations:
**the RS's (`mockapi`/Java/Micronaut) responses are exactly 1 byte
shorter in the `Date` header on any run that falls on days 1
through 9 of any month** (no leading zero on the day -- Decision 24).
This is **purely calendar-based**, not v8-vs-v9, not run to run --
confirmed in both directions (Decision 24). **Handling
adopted:** (a) each run's real date is already recorded
(`start_utc`/`end_utc`, per call, always logged -- no change
needed) -- any 1-byte discrepancy is retroactively explainable just
by checking that date, never mysterious;
(b) criterion 1's tolerance (Decision 20, ±50B on the Certificate)
already comfortably absorbs this ±1B in the TLS messages -- it is not
a risk to criterion 1 itself (which measures TLS, not the RS's HTTP
body); the risk is only for a future comparison of HTTP BODY SIZE
between runs on days with different digit counts, which needs to know
this caveat to avoid confusing it with a real regression.

**CAN the official campaign cross this boundary?** Yes, realistically
-- the fleet estimate (Decision 24, item 5) is ~29.9h continuous, but
the real v8 ran across MULTIPLE windows over >1 calendar day
(boot 2026-10-30T21:08, destroy 2026-10-31T19:36 -- almost 23h of
wall-clock time, not just active fleet-time) -- a similar pattern in
v9 could easily cross the turn of a 2-digit day into a 1-digit one
(e.g., day 30/31 into day 1) or vice versa. **How to handle it:**
there is no need to PREVENT the crossing (item (a) above already
makes it traceable) -- but, as a simple, zero-cost precaution,
**recorded as a scheduling recommendation**: avoid starting the
official campaign within ~2 days of a 9->10 or 30/31->1 turnover,
when the estimated duration is close to 24h+, simply to keep ALL 960
runs on the same side of the boundary and eliminate this variable
entirely instead of just explaining it afterward. If the crossing
happens anyway (e.g., real duration longer than estimated), item (a)
guarantees nothing is left unexplained.

**4. COST -- regional sensitivity added; the price source (a
third-party aggregator, not AWS's official table) made explicit; the
campaign estimate (anchored on v8's real spend) already reflects the
real regional mix, the pilot's (bottom-up) needed the adjustment.**

Billing Console) before any real campaign `apply`** -- it is not a
price guarantee, it is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

**Regional sensitivity, added:** `v8/DECISIONS.md` itself

more expensive regions (`sa-east-1`, `ap-northeast-*`), not
independently confirmed" about the cited `m7i-flex.large` rate
(US$0.0958/h is the `us-east-1` rate). **This matters more for the
PILOT than for the campaign:** given the real route structure

(L0/L219/L325) PLUS the server PLUS the control instance are ALL in

(conservative, the top of the range v8 already recorded) on compute:
- Compute: (4 x 0.0958x1.5 + 1 x 0.0084x1.5) x 2h ≈ US$1.17 (before:
  US$0.78 with no regional adjustment)
- Adjusted subtotal: ≈ US$1.27. **With a 30% margin: ≈ US$1.65.**
  Still **fits within US$27.72 with a large margin** (~6% of the cap).

**For the official campaign, the regional adjustment is NOT needed in

-- no change to this conclusion from this item, only the number's

**2. TAGS ACROSS ALL REGIONS -- fixed, `resourcegroupstaggingapi` is
regional by nature.**

Correct -- this API does not aggregate across regions, each call only
sees the region of the endpoint used. **Fixed in the procedure: the
verification before AND after each destroy runs across the pilot's 3
regions (`sa-east-1`, `eu-north-1`, `ap-southeast-1`), one call per
region, expecting empty in all 3** -- not just in the control
instance's region. **Additionally, once at the end of the entire
pilot (not per block):** run the same verification across ALL regions
enabled on the account (`aws account list-regions` or the fixed region
list v8 already used, 7-8 known regions), as a safety net against any
resource accidentally created in an unplanned region -- the same logic
as the real v8's final teardown (Decision 117, "confirmed via AWS's
real API across the 7 regions").

**3. SSH AND PKI -- complete operator-control-instances path
described, the private key never leaves the control instance without
being deleted, the control instance destroyed at the end.**

Looked up directly in v8's Decision 49 (real two-key architecture) and
applied to v9's PKI/binary/collection flow:

- **Entry path:** the operator connects DIRECTLY to the control
  instance (the control instance's elastic IP only accepts SSH from
  the operator's /32, Decision 49). The operator does NOT reach the
  server/clients directly -- each of them only accepts SSH from the
  CONTROL instance's own elastic IP (never the operator's). The
  control instance is the only intermediate hop to both sides.
- **PKI delivery:** the operator `scp`s each client's (L0/L219/L325)
  certificate/key + the public CA + the server's certificate/key,
  from the operator's machine to the control instance, using the
  OPERATOR's key (the same entry connection). The control instance,
  using the campaign's EXCLUSIVE key (generated by Terraform, never
  committed -- the same mechanism as Decision 49), `scp`s each piece
  to the right destination (the server receives its own material +
  the public CAs; each client receives ITS OWN certificate/key + the
  same public CAs).
- **Binary delivery:** the same path -- the operator `scp`s the
  `gateway`/`proxy` (plus the `.sha256`) to the control instance, the
  control instance `scp`s it to each destination instance (amd64 for
  the server+3 clients); each instance runs `sha256sum -c` before
  using it.
- **Per-block artifact collection:** reversed direction -- each
  instance (server/clients) `scp`s its own block artifacts to the
  control instance (campaign key), the control instance `scp`s them
  to the operator (operator's key); SHA-256 checked on each leg before
  deleting the remote original, exactly as Decision 24, item 2,
  already proposed (now with the 2-hop path made explicit, not
  implicit).
- **No private key is logged or persisted beyond what is necessary on
  the control instance:** each client/server's private key exists on
  the control instance's disk only between the incoming `scp` and the
  outgoing `scp` to its final destination -- deleted (`shred`)
  immediately after successful delivery to that destination is
  confirmed (the same `trap ... EXIT` pattern Decision 49 already
  uses for the campaign's SSH key, applied here also to the
  client/server mTLS keys). No `scp`/`cat`/`cp` command involving key
  material is printed with the key in clear text in any shell log --
  only the file name, never the content.
- **The control instance IS destroyed at the end of the pilot**,
  along with the server and the 3 clients -- confirmed in the
  destruction list (item 1 above, tag verification covers the control
  instance's region too). **The OPERATOR's copy (outside any AWS
  instance) is the ONLY one that persists until the entire pilot
  ends** (Decision 23, item 1) -- the copy inside the control instance
  is always ephemeral (deleted after each successful relay), never the
  "long" copy that item 1 describes.

## 27. Server address (EIP allocated before the instance, used in the SAN) and security group defined; read-only pre-flight with exact commands; abort procedure described; pre-registration check for push/tag -- real finding (a false positive from the command itself, fixed) that there is no private key in the v9 branch's history

**1. SERVER ADDRESS -- elastic IP, allocated BEFORE the instance;
used directly in the SAN; security groups defined.**

**Elastic (EIP), not DNS.** v9's own certificate generator
(`certs/main.go`, `-server-ips` flag) was already designed for this:
"in the real campaign, the fleet's IPs resolved at deploy time" (the
flag's comment, line 474). An Elastic IP can be ALLOCATED (`aws_eip`,
without the `instance` attribute) even before the instance exists --
this solves the ordering problem (the server's address is needed to
generate the server's cert, but the instance only comes up afterward)
with no need for DNS (hosted zone, propagation, TTL -- extra
infrastructure this project has never used anywhere). **Sequence:**
1) Terraform allocates the server's EIP (not yet associated) -- the
resulting address is an output; 2) that output feeds the single PKI
generator call (Decision 22/23, `-server-ips=<server's EIP>`),
producing the server's certificate with that exact IP as the SAN; 3)
the server instance comes up; 4) the EIP is associated to it. **The
server's SAN uses the IP, not a DNS name** -- IPs in a SAN are
fixed-width OCTET STRINGs (Decision 20, 4B IPv4), so they add no size
variability depending on the real IP, unlike a DNS name.

**Server's security group, defined:**
- Port 443: 3 ingress rules, one per client -- L0 via its PRIVATE IP
  (co-located in the same region/AZ, same pattern as the real v8,
  Decision 49), L219 and L325 via their respective public ELASTIC IP
  (different regions, no peering/VPN between regions in this
  infrastructure -- only the public IP reaches). Same pattern as the
  real v8: "one ingress rule per client, created once by Terraform."
- Port 22: ONE rule, only the CONTROL instance's elastic IP -- never
  the operator directly (Decision 26, item 3).
- **No IP is versioned in any file.** The addresses (the server's
  EIP, the 3 clients' EIPs, the control instance's EIP) only exist as
  RESOLVED values in `terraform.tfstate` (local, gitignored -- the
  same policy the real v8 already uses, Decision 49) and as computed
  variables inside Terraform itself (`aws_eip.*.public_ip`,
  referenced by another resource, never copied into a versioned `.tf`
  literal). The SG rules reference these computed values directly --
  Terraform's own dependency order resolves it (EIP allocated -> SG
  rule references the resulting IP -> both in the same apply, no
  manual round-trip).

**2. PRE-FLIGHT -- read-only, exact commands, Luciano's go/no-go
point before the first apply.**

**Go/no-go point: Luciano reviews each command's output and
